title: ESSAY 9: Basel III Norms and Their Impact on Indian Banks

blocks.content: (Word Count: ~280 words | Type: Descriptive-Analytical | Level: CBO / IBPS SO / RBI Grade B)

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Basel III norms were introduced by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) to strengthen banking regulation, risk management, and governance globally.
The framework rests on three pillars: Minimum Capital Requirements, Supervisory Review Process, and Market Discipline.
RBI prescribed a higher minimum Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) of 9% for Indian banks compared to the global standard of 8%.
It introduced key liquidity buffers including the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR).
Full implementation enhances the resilience of Indian Public and Private Sector Banks against systemic financial shocks.

blocks.content: The primary objective of Basel III is to improve the banking sector's ability to absorb shocks arising from financial and economic stress, whatever the source.

The global financial crisis of 2008, triggered by the collapse of systematically under-capitalised financial institutions in the United States and Europe, exposed fundamental weaknesses in the pre-crisis banking regulatory framework. In response, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) developed Basel III — a comprehensive reform package designed to strengthen the regulation, supervision, and risk management of the global banking sector. India's Reserve Bank of India began implementing Basel III from April 2013, with full implementation achieved by March 2019.

Basel III's most significant reform was the dramatic improvement in the quality and quantity of regulatory capital that banks must hold against their risk-weighted assets. It introduced the concept of Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital — the highest quality capital comprising paid-up equity and retained earnings — and mandated that banks hold minimum CET1 of 4.5% globally (raised to 5.5% in India) and total Tier 1 capital of 6% (7% in India). The Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB) of 2.5% added on top of the minimum 9% requirement means Indian banks must effectively maintain CRAR of 11.5% — significantly above the global minimum. The leverage ratio — limiting total exposures to a maximum of 25 times Tier 1 capital — prevents the excessive leverage that fuelled the 2008 crisis.

For Indian banks, particularly public sector banks, Basel III compliance has necessitated substantial capital infusion. The government injected over Rs. 3.10 lakh crore into PSBs through recapitalisation bonds between 2016 and 2022 to meet both NPA provisioning needs and Basel III capital requirements. Basel III's liquidity standards — the LCR and NSFR — have also reshaped bank balance sheet management, increasing holdings of high-quality liquid assets and promoting stable funding structures.

items: RBI mandates a minimum CAR of 9% for Indian banks, which is stricter than the 8% required under international Basel III guidelines.
Tier 1 Capital represents core capital (equity and disclosed reserves), while Tier 2 Capital acts as supplementary capital.
LCR measures short-term 30-day liquidity resilience, whereas NSFR ensures medium-to-long term structural funding stability over a 1-year horizon.

blocks.content: The outcome of Basel III compliance has been a more resilient Indian banking system. CRAR of Indian SCBs stood at approximately 16.8% in March 2024 — well above regulatory minimums — providing a substantial buffer against unexpected shocks. As Basel IV (the finalisation of the post-crisis reforms) phases in globally, Indian banks will need to continue evolving their capital and risk management frameworks, ensuring that strength, not complacency, defines India's banking future.

Examiner's Tip: Basel III essays require specific numbers: 4.5% CET1 globally vs 5.5% India; 2.5% CCB; 9% minimum CRAR; 16.8% actual CRAR. These details immediately distinguish a serious candidate from a surface-level one.
